Ajahn, how does recognising impermanence (anicca) free us from suffering?

Ajahn Sumedho points to impermanence directly: *"poly words or English or Thai but the words are impermanent and creations of the human mind they're not real dharma when we talk about talking about dhamma the whole point of talking about dhamma is to encourage trusting awareness that's how we realize dhamma is

ultimately As ultimate reality is is what we are here and now and apparent and timeless."* All conditioned phenomena — every thought, mood, sensation, and worldly situation — share the three characteristics: they are impermanent (anicca), unsatisfactory (dukkha), and selfless (anattā). When we fully receive this truth in the body rather than merely thinking about it, grasping naturally releases. It is like holding a hot coal: insight into anicca is the realisation that opens the hand. Right now, notice any thought or feeling present: watch it change without interference.

Ajahn, how do we meet suffering (dukkha) with awareness rather than resistance?

In this talk, Ajahn addresses suffering: *"You know when I first read that before I really developed meditation I thought well

life is s there's a lot of suffering all going on."* The First Noble Truth is not pessimism — it is the courageous acknowledgement: 'This is dukkha.' When we stop fighting unpleasant experience and simply know it with kind, patient awareness (sati), the suffering diminishes naturally. The wound heals fastest when kept clean and left in open air; resisting pain only tightens the knot. Bring gentle attention to wherever tension lives in your body right now.

Ajahn, what does it mean to rest in pure awareness rather than being lost in thought?

Ajahn Sumedho offers this pointer: *"We can observe sense

consciousness is pure consciousness."* Pure awareness (Buddho — the knowing quality) is the silent background against which all thoughts, emotions, and perceptions appear and dissolve. It is not produced by effort; it is what we already are before mental commentary begins. The practice is simply to notice the noticing — the aware space itself — rather than chasing the objects appearing within it. In this very moment, rest in the knowing that is reading these words.

Ajahn, this talk mentions mindfulness (sati). Can you explain this in the context of practice?

In this talk, the teaching on mindfulness (sati) — clear, present-moment awareness arises naturally from the investigation of present experience. Rather than taking this as a concept to memorise, use it as a mirror: where do you notice sati showing up right now in your body, mood, or thought? The Dhamma is not a philosophy to be studied from outside but a living reality to be seen clearly from within the laboratory of awareness. Let this teaching dissolve into direct knowing.
